Results are strings of JSON; parse.I searched every claim. The search tool then hit its usage limit, so I couldn't run a second, more authoritative search for claims 0 and 1. Claim 0 rests on commercial soil-weight pages and a textbook chapter whose text I only saw in part. Claim 1 rests on a magazine and secondary sites, with no official Cheyenne Mountain or Air Force page.

**Claim 0: Saturated soil weighs over 100 lb/ft³ (about 110–130).** Supported, with a note that the range depends on soil type.
- A hydrovac contractor's reference lists saturated clay at 130 lbs per cubic foot. Source: https://hydrovacattm.com/blogs/info/1-cu-ft-soil-weight
- A topsoil supplier gives saturated topsoil at 96–111 lbs per cubic foot, which is not over 100 at the low end. Source: https://topsoil.com/blog/how-much-does-a-cubic-yard-of-topsoil-weigh/
- Das, *Principles of Geotechnical Engineering* (Ch. 3), uses lb/ft³ for unit weight and has worked saturated-soil problems. The search excerpt didn't show its typical saturated values. Source: https://demo.webassign.net/dasprincgeoeng10si/Das_10e_SI_Ch_3.pdf
- Verdict: "over 100 lb/ft³" holds for most soils, but saturated organic or topsoil can be slightly under 100. "About 110–130" is a fair typical range. A safer wording is "roughly 100 to 130 lb/ft³ for most saturated soils."

**Claim 1: Cheyenne Mountain blast doors weigh about 25 tons each and are about 3 feet thick.** Supported as written, with some caution.
- Smithsonian Air & Space says the two steel blast doors each weigh 25 tons and measure three feet thick. The excerpt cuts off after "three". Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/06_sep2018-norad-at-1-180969908/
- Other sites give different numbers: roughly 20 to 25 tons each and about a meter, or approximately three and a half feet, thick. Source: https://everything-everywhere.com/the-cheyenne-mountain-complex/
- Another says 3.5 feet thick and around 23 tons. Source: https://envzone.com/cheyenne-mountain-complex-the-pinnacle-of-security/
- Verdict: "about 25 tons, about 3 feet thick" matches the best source I found. Because the figures vary, "roughly 25 tons and 3 or more feet thick" would be safer.

**Claim 2: Three feet of packed soil cuts gamma radiation about 1000-fold (ten half-value layers of 3.6 inches).** Supported, with a caveat that other civil-defense material gives a thicker figure.
- A shielding table lists packed soil with a halving thickness of 3.6 inches and a PF1000 thickness of 36.0 inches. It states about 36 inches, or 3 feet, achieves approximately PF1000. It also notes that multiplying the halving thickness by 10 gives a PF of about 1000 (1024). Source: https://modernsurvivalblog.com/nuclear/nuclear-radiation-shielding-protection/ (a blog, so it is weaker than the sources you asked for).
- The TACDA civil-defense basics course says ten half-value thicknesses of earth give a PF of 1,000 and need about 48 inches of earth cover. It also says forty inches of dirt gives the required 10 doublings. Its own figures disagree: 48 inches implies about 4.8 inches per layer, and 40 inches implies about 4 inches. Source: https://tacda.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/TACDA_Academy_CDBasics_6Radiation.pdf
- Verdict: the arithmetic of ten halvings giving about 1000 is right (2¹⁰ = 1024). The 3.6-inch value comes from a blog, and the older civil-defense course uses about 4 inches or more. A corrected form is "about 3 to 4 feet of packed earth (half-value layer roughly 3.6 to 4.8 inches) cuts gamma radiation about 1000-fold." I couldn't retrieve a primary government table in the search.

**Claim 3: By the 7-10 rule, about 49 hours after a blast, fallout radiation falls to roughly 1% of its one-hour level.** Supported as written.
- TACDA describes the seven-ten rule as a rule of thumb. It applies only to fallout of the same effective age. Source: https://tacda.org/radiation-issues/
- Another source gives the rule as for every sevenfold increase in time after the blast, radiation levels decrease by a factor of ten, citing FEMA. Source: https://protocolsurvival.com/en/blog/nuclear-fallout-preparedness
- A fallout-radiation presentation says at 7 hours after detonation, fission product activity falls to about 10%. Source: http://www.falloutradiation.com/johnwayne7
- Other sources say at about 49 hours, the dose rate is roughly 1% of its 1-hour value (https://phaenyx.com/guides/fallout-7-10-rule). The arithmetic is 1 h → 7 h (10%) → 49 h (1%).
- Verdict: supported. The script should call it a rule of thumb, since it is approximate and assumes fallout of the same effective age.
